reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Flexor tendon injuries are described by anatomical zones, and zone II (within the fibro-osseous flexor sheath, historically 'no man's land') is the most technically challenging because both flexor tendons run within a tight sheath
Examination should test flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis separately, as one may be intact while the other is divided
The resting cascade of the fingers is disrupted when a tendon is cut, and loss of the normal flexion posture on inspection is an important clue
Associated digital nerve and vessel injuries are common because of their proximity to the tendons and should be actively sought
Partial lacerations may retain some active movement but can still catch, rupture, or trigger, so they require careful assessment
Repair aims for a strong core suture with an epitendinous suture to allow early controlled motion, and preservation of key pulleys (particularly A2 and A4) prevents bowstringing
Structured early rehabilitation with a hand therapist is critical, balancing tendon glide against the risk of rupture, using controlled active or passive motion protocols
The main complications are adhesions causing stiffness, repair rupture, and joint contracture, and delayed presentation may require staged grafting or tendon reconstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Flexor tendons transmit force from forearm muscles to flex the digits and glide within synovial sheaths and beneath a series of annular and cruciate pulleys that hold them close to bone. Laceration divides the tendon and causes proximal retraction of the cut end, particularly when the muscle is contracting at the time of injury. Healing occurs through both intrinsic mechanisms, from tenocytes and synovial nutrition, and extrinsic mechanisms, through ingrowth of surrounding tissue that forms adhesions. Excessive extrinsic healing produces adhesions that restrict glide, while inadequate healing or excessive load risks gap formation and rupture. Within the confined zone II sheath, even small amounts of scarring markedly impair function.
additionalDifferentials: Extensor tendon injury or combined flexor-extensor injury
Digital nerve injury without tendon division
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical testing of profundus and superficialis function in each digit
Assessment of digital nerve sensation and vascular status
Plain radiographs to detect fractures, foreign bodies, or bony avulsion
Ultrasound or MRI to localise a retracted tendon end or characterise closed or partial injuries
Surgical exploration, which remains definitive for confirming and treating suspected injury
redFlags: Associated neurovascular injury threatening digital viability requiring urgent exploration
Signs of flexor sheath infection following an open injury (a surgical emergency)
Complete loss of active flexion with a retracted tendon needing timely repair before further retraction
Devascularised or grossly contaminated wound requiring prompt surgical management
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the zone of injury, associated damage, quality of repair, and adherence to rehabilitation. Zone II injuries carry the highest risk of adhesions and stiffness. With sound repair and supervised early motion, many patients regain good function, but adhesions, rupture, and contracture can necessitate tenolysis or staged reconstruction and may leave lasting deficits.
pitfalls: Failing to test profundus and superficialis separately and missing a partial or isolated tendon division
Overlooking associated digital nerve or vessel injury
Damaging or dividing critical pulleys (A2, A4), leading to bowstringing
Immobilising rather than starting an appropriate early motion protocol, causing dense adhesions
Being too aggressive with rehabilitation and precipitating repair rupture
Delaying repair so that tendon retraction complicates later reconstruction
management: Primary surgical repair with a strong multi-strand core suture and an epitendinous suture, preserving the A2 and A4 pulleys to prevent bowstringing
Concurrent repair of associated digital nerve and vessel injuries identified at exploration
Early controlled-motion rehabilitation under a specialist hand therapist with a protective dorsal blocking splint
Staged tendon reconstruction or grafting for delayed presentation, failed repair or segmental tendon loss
Tenolysis for restrictive adhesions limiting glide once healing is established and passive motion preserved
Hand-surgery and hand-therapy multidisciplinary follow-up to monitor for rupture, adhesions and contracture
